d: Sofas, beds, dining sets, desks and storage. The best months to buy, what a real discount looks like, where to look and this month’s buy-or-wait signal.
x: Furniture runs on a twice-a-year clock. New collections reach showrooms in February and August, so retailers spend January and July clearing the floor. That makes the weeks before each changeover the most reliable window for sofas, dining sets and bedroom furniture, with Presidents’ Day, Memorial Day, Labor Day and Black Friday layered on top. The headline discount matters less than the comparison price. Large furniture sellers are permanently “on sale”, so judge a deal against what the same piece sold for over the previous two or three months, and against the open-box and outlet versions of it. d: Mattresses, bases, toppers and bed-in-a-box brands. The best months to buy, what a real discount looks like, where to look and this month’s buy-or-wait signal.
x: Mattress pricing is built around four long weekends: Presidents’ Day, Memorial Day, Labor Day and Black Friday. Outside those windows most brands still run a promotion, but the holiday offers tend to add the extras that carry real value, such as a free base, pillows or a longer trial. Comparison shopping is deliberately hard. Many stores sell the same mattress under an exclusive model name, so match on construction instead: height, coil count, foam layers and firmness. For online brands, the trial period and return cost matter as much as the price. d: Refrigerators, ranges, dishwashers, washers and dryers. The best months to buy, what a real discount looks like, where to look and this month’s buy-or-wait signal.
x: Most major appliances are refreshed in the fall. Manufacturers release new ranges, dishwashers, washers and dryers around September and October, and retailers discount the outgoing models to clear them. Refrigerators are the exception: new models arrive in spring, so May is their month. The best total price usually comes from stacking. Holiday events add bundle savings for buying two or more pieces from one brand, retailers price-match each other, and utility rebates for efficient models can still apply even though the federal energy tax credits ended on December 31, 2025. x: Small appliances and cookware are gift categories, so prices fall hardest when retailers compete for gift spending: Black Friday week, the December run-up, and the big midsummer and October online sale events. These are also the products most often sold in slightly different versions for different stores. A stand mixer with a different bowl or a cookware set with one fewer pan can make a price look lower than it is. Compare by what is in the box. x: Tool deals follow gifting and project seasons. Father’s Day in June and the stretch from Black Friday to Christmas bring the combo-kit promotions, while home improvement stores run a spring event in April aimed at the start of project season. The pattern to know is the battery platform. Brands discount kits with batteries heavily and bare tools lightly, and they run “buy a starter kit, get a free tool” offers that beat any straight percentage. Buy into one platform and add bare tools later. d: Patio furniture, grills, mowers and garden equipment. The best months to buy, what a real discount looks like, where to look and this month’s buy-or-wait signal.
x: Outdoor products are the clearest example of buying against the season. Stores need the floor space for holiday stock by October, so patio sets, grills and mowers drop from late August, and the markdowns deepen every few weeks until the stock is gone. Spring sales look generous but mostly discount accessories and plants. For a large purchase such as a dining set, a gas grill or a riding mower, late summer and early fall win, as long as you accept a narrower choice of colours and sizes. x: Smart home devices are priced by the companies that make the platforms, and they use hardware discounts to win households. The lowest prices cluster around the big midsummer and October online sale events and Black Friday week, when doorbells, cameras, speakers and thermostats often fall by a third or more. Check the ongoing cost before the purchase price. d: Sheets, towels, comforters and bathroom basics. The best months to buy, what a real discount looks like, where to look and this month’s buy-or-wait signal.
x: January “white sales” are one of the oldest traditions in retail, and they still work: sheets, towels and comforters are discounted across department stores and home retailers for most of the month. August brings a second round aimed at students, with twin and twin XL sizes cheapest. Thread count is a poor guide to quality. Fibre and weave tell you more, and a 300-count long-staple cotton sheet will outlast an 800-count blend. Compare the same fibre, the same weave and the same size. x: Decor follows the same two-season rhythm as furniture, with clearance in January and July. Rugs are close to permanently discounted online, so the real signal is a price well under the level the rug has held for the past few months. Seasonal decor is the easy win. Holiday items fall by half or more in the days after the holiday, and artificial trees, lights and outdoor displays bought on December 26 are the cheapest they will be all year. x: Buy heating in spring and cooling in fall. Portable and window air conditioners are cleared from late August, space heaters from March, and both cost the most during the first hot or cold week of the season, when stock is short. For a full system replacement the same logic applies to labour. HVAC contractors are busiest in midsummer and midwinter. Schedule a replacement for early spring or fall and you gain time to compare quotes, which is where most of the saving comes from. d: Roofing: typical costs ($5,500 to $16,000), what moves the price, how to compare quotes and a free quote request with an instant ballpark.
x: $5,500 to $16,000 Typical asphalt-shingle replacement on an average home. A roof is priced by the square, which is 100 square feet of roof surface, and by what has to come off before the new one goes on. Two quotes for the same house can differ by thousands because one includes tearing off the old layers, replacing rotten decking and new flashing, and the other does not. That is why a roofing quote is only comparable when the scope is written down. Ask every roofer to price the same material, the same underlayment and the same tear-off, then compare warranties and how each handles decking that turns out to be damaged. t: Solar panels: costs and free quotes
d: Solar panels: typical costs ($16,000 to $26,000), what moves the price, how to compare quotes and a free quote request with an instant ballpark.
x: $16,000 to $26,000 Typical 6 to 8 kw home system before any state or utility incentive. Solar is sold by the watt. Divide the total price by the system size in watts and you can compare any two quotes: most residential installs land between about $2.50 and $3.50 per watt before incentives, and marketplaces that collect several bids report that shoppers who compare quotes pay meaningfully less than those who take the first offer. The incentive picture changed in 2026. The federal residential clean energy credit no longer applies to systems bought after December 31, 2025, so payback now depends on your electricity rate, your utility’s export rules and any state or utility program. Ask each installer to show the payback without assuming a federal credit. x: $4,500 to $16,000 Typical range from a single unit to a full heat pump system. HVAC prices swing with equipment size, efficiency and what the installer has to change around it. Ducts, the electrical panel, the refrigerant line set and the thermostat can each add to a quote, and they are the first things to check when one bid is far below the others. The right size matters more than the brand. Ask for a load calculation, known as a Manual J, instead of a like-for-like swap. Oversized equipment costs more, runs in short cycles and controls humidity poorly. d: Windows: typical costs ($450 to $1,400 per window), what moves the price, how to compare quotes and a free quote request with an instant ballpark.
x: $450 to $1,400 per window Installed, depending on frame material and glass. Window quotes are famous for high-pressure tactics: a large “list” price, a same-day discount and a manager’s call. The antidote is a per-window price in writing from at least three companies, for the same frame material, glass package and installation method. Installation method is the hidden variable. An insert replacement keeps the existing frame and costs less. A full-frame replacement removes everything to the studs, costs more and is the right answer when the old frame is rotten. Material choice sets the baseline, and removal of the old siding, house wrap and repairs to the sheathing set the rest. Ask how each installer handles water. d: Bathroom remodel: typical costs ($9,000 to $30,000), what moves the price, how to compare quotes and a free quote request with an instant ballpark.
x: $9,000 to $30,000 Typical full remodel of a standard bathroom. Bathrooms cost more per square foot than any other room because every trade works in a small space: plumbing, electrical, tile, ventilation and waterproofing. Moving a drain or a toilet is the single biggest multiplier, so the cheapest remodel keeps fixtures where they are. Allowances are where bathroom quotes diverge. One contractor may allow $4 per square foot for tile and another $12. Ask for the allowance on tile, vanity, fixtures and glass, and compare those before you compare totals. x: $18,000 to $60,000 Typical full remodel, mid-range finishes. Cabinets are the kitchen budget. They usually account for a third or more of the total, followed by labour, countertops and appliances. Contractors can only price what is drawn, and a quote built on a vague plan will grow through change orders. A simple measured layout and a list of finishes is enough to get comparable numbers. x: $900 to $2,500 Typical local move of a two or three bedroom home. Local moves are billed by the hour and long-distance moves by weight and distance. t: How to tell a real deal from a fake discount
d: Five checks that separate a genuine price drop from an inflated “was” price, with a calculator that does the arithmetic.
x: In short A discount only means something against the price people actually paid. Unit price, delivery and required add-ons decide the real cost. If a product is always on sale, the sale price is the price. A red tag tells you what a retailer wants you to compare. It does not tell you whether the price is good. The percentage on a sale sign is calculated from a reference price the seller chose, and that reference price is the weakest number on the page. Start with the price that was actually charged U.S. advertising rules say a former price used in a comparison should be one at which the product was genuinely offered for a reasonable period. In practice many home products spend most of the year “on sale”. A sofa listed at $1,999 and sold at $1,199 every week is a $1,199 sofa. So check the history. Look at what the same item sold for over the past two or three months, at the same store and

t: Why home prices follow a calendar, and how to use it
d: Model years, floor space and weather set the price of furniture, appliances and outdoor goods. Here is the logic behind the best months to buy.
x: In short Retailers discount when they need space, not when you need the product. Buy against the season: cooling in fall, heating in spring, patio at summer’s end. Holiday weekends are strongest for mattresses and major appliances. Sale calendars look like folklore until you see what drives them. Three forces set the timing of almost every home discount, and once you know them you can predict the low point for a product nobody has written a calendar for. Force one: the model year Manufacturers refresh product lines on a schedule. Most major appliances are renewed in September and October, refrigerators in May, furniture collections in February and August, and vacuums in early summer. The weeks before a refresh are when retailers cut prices on the outgoing version, which is usually the same product with last year’s handle. Force two: floor space A store can only display so much. t: Black Friday for the home: what to buy and what to skip
d: Which home categories genuinely hit their yearly lows in Black Friday week, which do not, and how to prepare a short list.
x: In short Best: small kitchen appliances, vacuums, smart home devices, tool kits and bedding-in-a-box mattresses. Wait: holiday decor, linens, furniture clearance and flooring installation. Sales now start in late October, so the price on the Friday itself is rarely special. Black Friday is no longer a day. Large home retailers now open “early” sales in late October and keep them running into December, which changes the job from queuing to comparing. The questions are which categories reach a true low in this window and how to recognise it. Categories that usually hit their lows Small kitchen appliances and cookware. Gift demand makes this the most competitive category of the season. Vacuums and robot vacuums. Previous-generation models fall furthest. Smart home devices. Platform makers discount their own hardware heavily. Tool combo kits. Look for free-tool offers with a battery starter

t: How to buy a major appliance for less
d: Model changeovers, bundle rebates, open-box stock and delivery terms: the levers that set the real price of a refrigerator, range or washer.
x: In short Outgoing models are cleared in September and October, refrigerators in May. Bundle offers, price matching and utility rebates stack. Delivery, installation parts and haul-away belong in the comparison. Appliance prices move more than most people expect. The same dishwasher can sell for 30% less in October than in March, and the gap between the advertised price and the delivered, connected price can be several hundred dollars. Here is how to control both. Buy the outgoing model New ranges, dishwashers, washers and dryers reach stores in September and October, and new refrigerators in May. Retailers discount the previous model to clear it. The differences are often cosmetic, so the outgoing model at 25% to 40% under its launch price is the standard good deal in this category. t: How to shop a mattress sale without getting lost in model names
d: Why mattresses are hard to compare, what the four holiday sales really offer, and the terms that matter more than the discount.
x: In short The same mattress is sold under different names at different stores. Compare construction, trial period, return cost and warranty. Presidents’ Day, Memorial Day, Labor Day and Black Friday are the four real sales. Mattresses are one of the few products designed to resist comparison. Manufacturers sell near-identical models under exclusive names to each retailer, which makes price matching almost impossible and leaves the shopper comparing adjectives. Compare the build, not the name Ask for, or look up, four facts about any mattress: its height, its type (innerspring, hybrid, foam or latex), the coil count and gauge if it has coils, and the thickness and density of its foam layers. Two mattresses that match on those are close relatives whatever they are called. Know the four sales Presidents’ Day in February, Memorial Day in May, Labor Day in September and Black Friday in Novembe

d: The discounted conditions explained, with a checklist for warranty, returns and inspection before you buy.
x: In short Open-box is a return, refurbished is repaired and tested, scratch-and-dent is cosmetically damaged. Who refurbished it and who backs the warranty matter more than the label. Inspect before delivery leaves, and check for recalls. Three labels cover most discounted non-new stock, and each means something different about what happened to the product before it reached you. What the labels mean Open-box. Bought, opened and returned, or used as a display. Often unused. Usually sold with the retailer’s normal return policy. Refurbished or renewed. New and working, with cosmetic damage from shipping or the warehouse floor. Floor model. Displayed in a store. Expect wear on touch points. The checklist Who stands behind it? t: Stacking savings: the order that gets the lowest price
d: Sale price, coupon, rebate, cashback, card offer and price adjustment: how they combine, and the order to apply them.
x: In short Discounts multiply in sequence, so 20% then 10% is 28%, not 30%. Portals and card offers pay on the amount you are charged. A price adjustment after purchase is the most overlooked saving. The lowest price on a home purchase rarely comes from one discount. It comes from five or six small ones applied in the right order. Each layer is modest, and together they regularly add 10% to 20% on top of the sale price. The stack, in order Sale price. Start from a price that is good against its own history. Stacking cannot rescue a bad base price. Store coupon or promo code. Email sign-up codes, loyalty offers and mover’s coupons from home improvement stores. Most stores accept one code per order. Manufacturer or utility rebate. Common on appliances, paint, water heaters and thermostats. Submit the same day and keep copies. Cashback portal. Click through before adding items to the basket.

t: How to compare contractor quotes line by line
d: A method for getting three comparable quotes, reading what is missing from each, and choosing on value instead of the bottom line.
x: In short Write one scope and give it to every contractor. The cheapest quote is often the one that left something out. Tie payments to finished stages, and keep the deposit small. Three quotes for the same job can differ by 50%. Usually nobody is cheating. Each contractor priced a different job, because each was given a different description of it. The fix is to control the description. Write the scope first One page is enough. State what is being done, where, with which materials or grade of material, what is being removed, and who handles permits and disposal. Send the same page to every contractor and ask them to price exactly that, with alternatives listed separately. Line the quotes up Put the quotes side by side and compare these lines: Materials. t: Home energy savings after the federal tax credits ended
d: The 25C and 25D credits stopped at the end of 2025. Here is what still pays: utility and state rebates, and the upgrades with the fastest payback.
x: In short Federal credits for home efficiency and residential clean energy ended for work done after December 31, 2025. Utility rebates and state-run programs still exist and vary by ZIP code. Air sealing, insulation and controls usually pay back before equipment does. For three years, federal tax credits covered 30% of many home energy upgrades. That changed with legislation signed in July 2025. According to the IRS, the Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit is not allowed for property placed in service after December 31, 2025, and the Residential Clean Energy Credit is not allowed for expenditures made after that date. What that means in practice Upgrades completed in 2025 or earlier could be claimed on that year’s return using Form 5695. t: Refinance math when rates are high
d: The break-even calculation, what points really cost, and the options for owners whose existing rate is lower than today’s.
x: In short Break-even months equal closing costs divided by monthly savings. If your current rate is below today’s average, a rate-and-term refinance cannot help. Compare at least three lenders on the same day, using the Loan Estimate. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was % in the week of , according to Freddie Mac’s weekly survey, compared with % a year earlier. Whether refinancing makes sense depends entirely on which side of that number your current loan sits. The break-even calculation Refinancing replaces your loan with a new one and costs money up front, commonly a few percent of the loan amount in lender fees, title, appraisal and prepaid items. The decision comes down to one division: Break-even months = total closing costs ÷ monthly payment savings If closing costs are $6,000 and the new payment is $200 lower, you break even in 30 months. Stay longer than that and you gain.

t: Check recalls before you buy clearance or secondhand
d: How product recalls work, where they are published, and a two-minute check for furniture, appliances and heaters.
x: In short It is illegal to sell a recalled consumer product in the U.S., including secondhand. Dressers, mattresses, heaters and battery-powered tools account for many home recalls. Recalled products usually qualify for a refund, repair or replacement. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission announces several hundred recalls a year, and a large share involve things found in every home: dressers that tip, mattresses that fail the flammability standard, heaters and fire pits that burn, and battery packs that overheat. Why clearance and secondhand need a check Selling a recalled product is against federal law, and that includes resale. In practice recalled items still circulate through marketplaces, garage sales and liquidation lots, because sellers often do not know. t: A first-year budget for a new homeowner
d: What to set aside for maintenance, which big-ticket items to plan for, and a seasonal checklist that prevents the expensive repairs.
x: In short Set aside 1% to 4% of the home’s value each year for maintenance and repairs. Know the age of the roof, water heater and HVAC, because they fail on a schedule. Small seasonal jobs prevent most large bills. The mortgage payment is the predictable part of owning a home. The unpredictable part is everything attached to it, and the first year is when most new owners discover what the previous owner postponed. How much to set aside A long-standing rule of thumb is 1% to 4% of the home’s value per year for maintenance and repairs, with newer homes at the low end and older homes at the high end. On a $400,000 house that is roughly $330 to $1,330 a month. You will not spend it evenly. Some years cost little and one year replaces a roof. t: Home repair scams and high-pressure sales: how to say no
d: The common patterns, your cancellation rights for sales made at your door, and what to do if something has already gone wrong.
x: In short A price that expires today is a sales tactic. Most sales of $25 or more made at your home can be cancelled within three business days. Never pay in full up front, and never sign over an insurance claim under pressure. Most contractors are honest. The dishonest ones are easy to recognise, because they use the same handful of approaches and they all depend on speed. Slowing the conversation down defeats nearly every one. The patterns The storm chaser. Arrives after hail or wind, offers a free inspection, finds damage and asks you to sign immediately. Leftover materials. A crew “just finished a job nearby” and can do your driveway or roof cheaply today, for cash. The today-only price. A large list price, a dramatic discount and a call to a manager.
